blocks.c: Martin Sheen is muddy and looks anxious in Apocalypse Now.

blocks.c: Aleksei Kravchenko as Flyora Gaishun, standing in front of a fire looking devastated in Come and See.

By the end, Florya looks decades older than he did at the beginning. That transformation is the argument. War has not made him a man but has stolen the child and left somebody else wearing his face.

blocks.c: Colonel Dax addressing someone off-camera in Paths of Glory

Men start humming along. Some cry. They do not understand all the words. They do not need to. For a few minutes, the uniforms stop mattering and everybody in that room is simply homesick. Then the soldiers are ordered back to the front.

'Apocalypse Now' (1979)

Apocalypse Now is flawless in a different way. It sends Captain Benjamin Willard (Martin Sheen) upriver during the Vietnam War with orders to find and kill Colonel Walter Kurtz (Marlon Brando), a decorated American officer who has abandoned military command and created his own violent kingdom deep in Cambodia.

Calling what follows a “mission” barely survives the first hour. On top of that, the film comes from Francis Ford Coppola (The Godfather) and we know he leaves no crumbs. Then there’s the character of Lieutenant Colonel Kilgore (Robert Duvall) who launches an attack on Wagner because he likes the surfing conditions nearby. A USO show involving Playboy Playmates collapses into chaos. A bridge is rebuilt every night simply so command can claim the road remains open. The farther Willard travels, the less war resembles anything with an objective. By the time Kurtz begins talking in the darkness about horror, you understand why the film has spent so long stripping away normal logic. The nightmare is not that Kurtz went insane. It is how much of the world around him already was.

'Come and See' (1985)

Image via Sovexportfilm

Come and See follows Florya (Aleksei Kravchenko), a Belarusian teenager who digs up a rifle and eagerly joins Soviet partisans during the Nazi occupation, imagining that he is entering some kind of adventure. The film then watches that idea get annihilated.

There are faces in this movie I genuinely wish I could forget. Elem Klimov helmed this film back in 1985 but did it brilliantly and he keeps bringing the camera painfully close to Florya as the boy’s expression ages faster than his body. After an explosion destroys his hearing, the soundtrack becomes a high ringing drone and the world seems to move several feet away from him. Then comes the village massacre, where civilians are herded into a building and burned alive while German soldiers treat the event with grotesque casualness. By the end, Florya looks decades older than he did at the beginning. That transformation is the argument. War has not made him a man but has stolen the child and left somebody else wearing his face.

'Paths of Glory' (1957)

Image via United Artists

Paths of Glory begins when French General Mireau (George Macready) orders soldiers to attack a heavily fortified German position during World War I, despite knowing the assault is almost certainly suicidal. When the attack fails, three men are selected to stand trial for cowardice so the military can pretend the disaster resulted from weak soldiers rather than catastrophic leadership.The battle is almost secondary. What makes the film vicious is what happens afterward.

Colonel Dax (Kirk Douglas) walks through trenches surrounded by frightened men, then later stands in a polished courtroom where their lives are being discussed as administrative inconveniences. The three defendants barely matter to the generals as individuals. They are examples. That is the obscenity. And then the film ends with something astonishingly tender. German singer Christiane (Susanne Christian) stands before a room of drunken French soldiers who initially mock her. She begins singing “The Faithful Hussar.” Slowly, the room goes quiet. Men start humming along. Some cry. They do not understand all the words. They do not need to. For a few minutes, the uniforms stop mattering and everybody in that room is simply homesick. Then the soldiers are ordered back to the front.
